posts.text:
I'm pretty sure I figured out the issue with the Harry Potter scene's bad color. TLDR: the HDR to SDR tonemap is incorrect, so the gamma is wrong. Here is the scene with the correct gamma. (No grading changes were made at all. Just a technical transform).

Ok, now for the long description: When you make a show in HDR, you need to properly tonemap the final grade to SDR in order to watch on an SDR device, or to share clips on social media (because most social media sites don't handle HDR well, or at all). 

Tonemapping is when you take a high dynamic range video source, and remap the color and luma values to fit within a standard dynamic range container. You're essentially "translating" a large format into a lesser format.

HDR in cinema/streaming typically has a gamut of Rec.2020 and a gamma (transfer function) of ST.2084. This needs needs to be converted down to Rec.709 Gamma 2.4.

The Rec.2020 gamut got converted to Rec.709 just fine, which is why the hues look correct in the original clip. But somebody forgot to do the other half of the conversion, which would be to take the ST.2084 transfer function and convert it down to Gamma 2.4. This explains why the contrast looks completely wrong in the original clip. Here's what it looks like when you tonemap the gamma.

NOTE: There are multiple ways to tonemap an image. Some ways handle high brightness and high saturation values better than others, and give you tools to dynamically adjust those values (this is what Dolby Vision is, in case you didn't know). The tonemap method I used for this demonstration is just a simple global one though, so the saturated values of the lamps would probably look better using a more robust/dynamic method.

Paul McCartney has spent fifty years telling the world to stop eating meat, and on this subject he is not a serious person.

He wrote Yesterday, so he is allowed almost anything. The trouble starts when he gets on to dinner.

He gave up meat in the 1970s after looking out of his farmhouse window at the lambs while eating one. He had, a few years before, released a single called Mary Had a Little Lamb.

He still keeps sheep on the farm in Scotland. None of them is ever eaten. They are shorn, they grow old, and they are buried. It is the only flock in Argyll run as a retirement home, and it is offered as a model for feeding eight billion people.

In 2009 he launched Meat Free Monday, to save the planet one day a week. He promoted it between world tours, which are conducted by private jet.

In 2008 Lexus gave him a hybrid limousine for his green credentials. It came from Japan. It was flown, 7,000 miles, because the boat would have taken too long. The carbon saved by the hybrid engine was spent about a hundred times over before he had sat in it.

He says that if slaughterhouses had glass walls everyone would be vegetarian. The frozen sausages sold under his late wife's name are made of rehydrated soya and rapeseed oil in a factory owned by an American conglomerate, and nobody has ever asked for a look round.

Last year he wrote to Brussels to defend the right of a vegetable to be called a burger.

So the position is that a sheep on a Scottish hill is a moral emergency, the jet is logistics, and the planet will be rescued on Mondays.

He has never, in fifty years, met a hill farmer he could not write a song about and then put out of business.
